(p-٣٨٧)Surah Sabbih, also called al-A'la (The Most High)

Al-Malawi said: The Prophet (ﷺ) [loved it - ] because of the great amount of knowledge and good it contains. Its purpose is to establish tanzih (declaring Allah free from every imperfection) for al-A'la (the Most High), glory be to Him and exalted be He, so that no trace of deficiency may reach the sanctity of His majesty. Such deficiencies include hastening in a matter, such as destroying the disbelievers or something else, or inability regarding resurrection, or leaving creation neglected and purposeless, so that some of them oppress others without accounting. Or they include speaking in a way that does not correspond to reality, or saying something that anyone could say in the same way. This is what at-Tariq indicated in summary, and this surah explained in detail. Each of its names indicates this: Sabbih and al-A'la. (In the name of Allah) the One to whom all loftiness belongs, so no deficiency reaches Him. (The Most Merciful) whose generosity encompasses all, so every existent is the one He brought into being, and every living creature is the one He nurtures and provides for. (The Most Compassionate) who, whoever belongs to His party, He obliges to obedience, makes it easy for him, and grants him success.

* *

(p-٣٨٨)Because the command of Allah, glory be to Him, at the end of at-Tariq included an instruction to be patient and a prohibition against hastening, which is exempt from Him because it would be a deficiency, and because the negation of jest concerning the Qur'an indicated that they had accused it of that while it is far from it, and because of other matters alluded to in it, He, the Most Holy, declared Himself exempt from these. He commanded His most perfect creation, the Messenger to whom this Qur'an was revealed (ﷺ), to declare the exaltation of His name, because He alone knows its true knowledge. When His name is declared exempt from being invoked for an idol or anything else, or from being placed where it does not befit, then His own essence, glory be to Him, is all the more exempt. So He said, encouraging remembrance, especially with tanzih, which is the negation of what is impossible for Him, because clearing away comes before adorning. He explained the foundations of religion, introducing the theology of divinity (ilahiyyat), which is the ultimate matter, beginning with the Essence, then the Attributes, especially al-Qayyumiyya (self-subsistence), then the Actions, and then prophethood. He then followed this with prophethood so that the servant may know his Lord as He is in His majesty and beauty. Thus the disease of ignorance, which leads to blind imitation (taqlid), and the disease of arrogance, which leads to denying rights, are removed from him, and he acknowledges servanthood and lordship. He does not praise Him, glory be to Him, only for His majesty and then His beauty, but worships Him as befits Him, by carrying out His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, glorifying His station. ﴿Glorify﴾ means: declare Him free from imperfection and clear Him, with a very great, strong and mighty declaration and clearing. ﴿the name of your Lord﴾ meaning the One who has been good to you after bringing you into being in the state of perfection, by nurturing you (p-٣٨٩) in the best of qualities, until you reached the utmost of majesty and beauty.

Since a human being, in order for his life to be good so that he can achieve what he wants, needs three things: a great one to whom he belongs, so that he gains elevation through him, which benefits him in his important affairs and protects him in his times of need; a model to whom he ties himself in his difficulties; and a best way that he follows, as indicated by the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "I am content with Allah as Lord, with Muhammad (ﷺ) as Prophet and Messenger, and with Islam as religion." He (ﷺ) was guided that attachment to Him is the highest rank. So He said, describing the One whom He commanded to be glorified, by affirming what belongs to Him of necessary attributes after negating what is impossible, as indicated by the words "Glory be to You and praise be to You": ﴿the Most High﴾, meaning the One who has the attribute of supremacy in rank, not in place in an absolute sense, free from every trace of deficiency and every evil of deviation (ilhad) in any of His names through corrupt interpretations (ta'wil), and from ascribing them to others while claiming that they are equal in Him. He mentioned Him without any glorification or other matters, so that the one who mentions Him may be firmly established in tanzih, and thus be among the people of gnosis (irfan), who give light to people while being, in their firmness, like lofty pegs, which, despite their height, do not move. Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned (p-٣٩٠) this meaning, expressing it through all its four aspects, at the beginning of four surahs, to encompass this noble word from all its aspects. He began Surah al-Isra, which is the surah of ihsan (excellence), with "Subhan" (Glory be to), a verbal noun suitable for all its meanings, to inform that this meaning is established for Him absolutely, not restricted by any time or other limitation. Then He repeated it in the past tense at the beginning of al-Hadid, al-Hashr and as-Saff, explicitly stating that what the verbal noun conveys has occurred in the past, which encompasses from eternity to the time of revelation. Then He used it a third time, in the present tense, at the beginning of al-Jumu'ah and at-Taghabun, so that it conveys, along with what the verbal noun and the past tense convey, the continuity of renewal. When this was complete from all its aspects, the command was directed, and this surah was specified with it. What completes this has already passed at the beginning of al-Hadid and al-Jumu'ah.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 87, verse 2:

Since origination (al-ibda') is the clearest proof of perfection together with transcendence (al-tanazzuh), especially light, which is the cause of disclosure and manifestation, and since this is an elaboration of His saying "from what He was created" (mimma khuliqa), and it is the strongest thing indicating the aforementioned resurrection "on the day when the hidden things are tested" (fi [yawmi -] tubla al-sara'ir), He said, clarifying the Agent whom He left vague because of its clarity in "from what He was created," encouraging reflection (al-fikr) upon His acts, glorified and exalted is He, which is the closest cause of happiness through indicating Him by what He has of possible acts, after encouraging remembrance (al-dhikr), which prepares for reflection: ﴿Who created﴾ (p-391), meaning He brought into existence from non-existence, meaning He possesses the attribute of origination for everything He wills, nothing being difficult for Him. ﴿And proportioned﴾, meaning He caused, together with origination and after it, proportioning in every creature, by making for it what allows its perfection to be realized and its livelihood to be completed, and He balanced among the four temperaments: water, air, and fire (and earth), after subduing them to be joined together despite their opposition, lest they corrupt one another. This is by complete knowledge and perfect power, indicating the completeness of His wisdom and that His act is by choice.

And Ustadh Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: When the Glorified and Exalted said, reporting about the blindness of the disbelievers in the darkness of their bewilderment, ﴿Indeed, they are plotting a plot﴾ [al-Tariq: 15], and that occurrence from servants, who are encompassed by their deeds and the subtleties of their breaths and states, is among the most evil of transgressions and the farthest from knowledge of anything of the great matter of the Creator, majestic is His majesty and exalted is His dignity, He, glorified be He, followed that with commanding His Prophet ﷺ to exalt his Lord, the Most High, above their vile transgression and their lying slander, saying ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-A'la: 1], meaning, declare Him free of their evil speech. He placed the alerting (al-tanbih) to transcendence before transcendence in such matters, their like, and their occurrence within the surahs [and -] among one surah and another. He, glorified and exalted is He, followed the introduction of His great power and perfect wisdom with what clarifies their error, saying ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾ ﴿and who determined and guided﴾ [al-A'la: 2-3] (p-392) ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14], and exalted is He above what the slanderers fabricate. End of quotation.

Since the arrangement of things at differing measures, together with guidance toward that for which each creature was made in differing ways, despite the equality of their elements, belongs to what follows the act of proportioning (taswiyah), and it is one of the distinctive attributes of the King, which is only possible with perfection, He followed it with it using the conjunction "and" (wa), to indicate the firm establishment of these attributes, and said: ﴿And He who measured﴾, that is, He set His measuring into the kinds of things, their types, their individual existences, their quantities, their attributes, their actions, their terms, and other conditions of them, so He made grasping for the hand, walking for the foot, hearing for the ear, sight for the eye, and the like. ﴿And guided﴾, that is, through His measuring and what follows from it, He brought about guidance for that for which the measuring was made, in its form, its substances, and its accidents, which He equipped it with suited to what befits it, naturally or by choice, by creating inclinations and inspirations, and by setting up proofs and signs to repel harms and bring about goods. Thus you see the infant, as soon as it emerges from the womb, opening its mouth for nursing, and other animals among all the rest of the creatures are guided to what benefits them among all the various benefits. So creation necessarily requires proportion so that balance is attained, and measuring necessarily requires guidance so that perfection is attained.

Since the proofs of tawhid (divine oneness) come sometimes through the self (nafs) and sometimes through the horizons (al-afaq), and he has alerted us through the signs of the self, only the signs of the horizons remain. Among these signs, vegetation is the most indicative of created things of resurrection (al-ba'th). So he said: ﴿And He who brought forth the pasture﴾, meaning, He who effected the bringing forth of the pasture ﴿by what He sent down of rain-laden clouds﴾, so that He caused to grow what the animals graze upon, of herbage and other plants, both at the beginning and in return. This indicates the completeness of His power, especially over resurrection, because He, glorified and exalted, is more capable of gathering the dead from the earth by Himself, after they have been scattered and turned to dust, than of gathering the plant, which had been scattered in the earth and became [dust], by means of water. Its bringing forth is as it was in the previous year, by His permission, glorified and exalted be He, and it is one of His created things.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 87, verse 5:

Since its drying out and turning black after its greening and growth is most clearly a sign of complete power and perfect choice, through the alternation of opposites in a single substance, God the Exalted says: ﴿Then He makes it﴾, that is, after stages of time from the moment of its emergence, ﴿stubble﴾, that is, abundant. Then He brings it to an end, dries it out, crushes it and tears it apart, so He gathers the flood, some of it onto some of it, and makes it foam, perishing, decaying and crumbled bits on the [face of -] earth, ﴿dark green﴾, that is, in the utmost state of lushness, until it becomes black tending toward green, or red tending toward black, or its greenness intensifies so that it becomes tending toward black. Al-Qazzaz, may God have mercy on him, said in his Diwan: "The ḥuwwa is a marking among the markings of horses, and it lies between the dark bay and the bay-black. This usage became common until they called every black thing aḥwā." End of quotation.

So it is permissible to mean here that it is black from the intensity of its dryness, so the winds gather it and bring it together from every direction, where it is crumbled. Each of the two words in it contains life and death. He placed the second one later because its indication of greenness is more complete; had it been placed first, it would not have been turned to anything else. Thus His combining of opposites in a single substance indicates complete choice. As for natural forces, they have only the affirmative influence with which God the Exalted established them, like fire: whenever it touches something it burns it, and after that it cannot transform it into another attribute other than the one you have imprinted on it. By "beginning" and "end" He points to remembering this, and that it occurs by way of repetition every year, which indicates the resurrection of creatures. The pasture is singled out because it is more indicative of resurrection, since it is something people grow; and when it ends it crumbles, breaks apart and becomes dust, and then God the Exalted restores it with water to what it was, [exactly as He does with the dead -] without any difference at all.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 87, verse 6:

When Allah, glorified and exalted, had completed the description of the one whom He commanded (ﷺ) to glorify Him, through what indicates the attributes of His beauty and the qualities of His greatness and majesty, and had explained what He possesses of complete power over origination, guidance, and disposing of spirits, both sensory and immaterial, by spreading out and folding up, by seizing and extending, He thereby indicated the perfection of the foundations of the religion, by way of proving His existence, glorified be He, in a descending manner from His essence to His attributes and then to His acts. Thus what belongs to the Creator was complete, and He followed it with what belongs to the creatures, beginning with the most noble of His creation, upon whom this Remembrance (the Qur'an) was sent down, honouring prophethood, by which happiness is completed through the realities that reach His servant from the Truth, and by which His command is completed in the two powers, the cognitive (ʿilmiyyah) and then the practical (ʿamaliyyah), by accepting the message after monotheism. For the life of a human being is not made good except by a model to be followed, in his sayings, his actions, and all his conditions, and there is no model like the one protected from every inclination, which makes that love due from every aspect that knows his state. And love for the sake of Allah is among the greatest pillars of the religion. So He said, giving the reason for the command to glorify the One described with majesty and beauty, indicating that He gives life to dead spirits with knowledge just as He gives life to dead bodies with spirits: ﴿We shall make you recite﴾, that is, We shall make you, by Our greatness, by a promise that admits no failure, through repetition, renewal and continuity, a reciter, that is, one who gathers this Remembrance, which is the life of spirits just as bodily life is the life of bodies, which you have made clear is a decisive word, knowing every knowledge through it, spreading it among every living being, distinguishing through it every ambiguous matter, even though you are unlettered, not skilled in writing or reading. Therefore He made the following a consequence of this: ﴿and you will not forget﴾, that is, not any part of it nor anything else, so that in this there would be two signs: your reciting while you are unlettered, and your reporting of the future, which then comes to pass as you said. ﴿So do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾, and do not exhaust yourself, for upon Us is its preservation in your breast and the making of your tongue utter it, at the time of revelation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 87, verse 7:

Since Allah, glorified and exalted be He, abrogates from the Sacred Law whatever He wills according to the interests (maslahat) involved, lightening the burden for this Ummah out of the gentleness He has toward it, He said, turning the speech away into the third-person mode (siyaq al-ghayba) to indicate that mentioning the Majesty (al-Jalalah) is greater than explicitly using a particle of greatness (adat al-azamah): ﴿Except what Allah wills﴾, that is, the Supreme King to whom all command belongs, [wills] that you forget it, because He has abrogated it; or so that His greatness may be manifest in that the greatest of creation is overcome by the Qur'an, since it is an attribute of Allah, so you forget the verse or the word and then remember it, sometimes by the reminder of one of the individuals of your Ummah and sometimes otherwise.

Since the one who does all these things, especially the teaching (al-iqra') and the judgment concerning what is recited, is such that He does not forget except what He wills to forget, and would not be [one whose knowledge is] encompassing unless... He said, explicitly stating this, emphasizing it in order to refute those of deficient vision who consider a like of Him, following the mode of the third person (uslub al-ghayba), expressing by the pronoun an indication of His exaltation in greatness to the point where the hopes of creation are cut off from comprehending Him, by the multitude of His acts: ﴿Indeed, He﴾, that is, the One who, whatever He wills, comes to be, ﴿Indeed, Our word to a thing when We intend it is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [an-Nahl: 40].

Since the purpose is to explain the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, glorified and exalted be He, and that the relation to Him of the manifest and the hidden, [namely] His loud recitation of the Qur'an and its repetition upon His heart in secret, and other things, is on one equal footing, and since the context concerned the manifest, He mentioned both explicitly, placing the manifest first (because this is its station), and He mentioned it with its description, expressing it by the name that indicates the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of it, so He said: ﴿He knows what is apparent﴾, that is, this description is established for Him in the manner of renewal and continuity in teaching, reciting and other things. And when He mentioned Him by His name so as to indicate that He knows it absolutely, not restricted to the condition of being loud, He said, stating this explicitly: ﴿and what is hidden﴾, that is, whose concealment continually renews from recitation and other things, in whatever state the concealment may be, which indicates His knowledge of it when it is made loud, all the more so.

When al-Biqa'i had mentioned the divine matters (al-Ilahiyyat) and prophethood, and an allusion had been made to abrogation (naskh), he pointed out that the religion prescribed for Him is the tolerant monotheistic faith (al-hanifiyyah al-samhah), and that He, glorified and exalted is He, does not establish it in any matter, whether through abrogation or otherwise, except that it is the easier [for Him] and the more gentle, because gentleness and harshness change according to the time. So He said, clarifying the practical faculty (al-quwwah al-amaliyyah) through the effect of His clarification of the cognitive faculty (al-quwwah al-ilmiyyah): ﴿And We will ease you﴾, that is, We will make you prepared, facilitated, softened, and successful ﴿for the easy way﴾, that is, in preserving and reflecting upon the revelation and in all the other paths and states, which are all gentle, easy, and light, as indicated by His saying: "Each is made easy for that for which he was created." For this reason He did not say, "And We will ease the way for you," because you are inherently disposed to love it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 87, verse 9:

When He (Allah, glorified and exalted be He) had perfected him (ﷺ) and prepared him for the easiest way and facilitated it for him to the utmost degree of facilitation, He made it a consequence of this that it became obligatory for him to remind every person in every state, perfecting others out of compassion for the creatures of Allah, after (perfecting) himself. For Allah has moments in which He sends forth breezes of grace (nafahat), in which needs are fulfilled. This is because he had become like the skilled physician in treating the sick, so he stands to benefit His servants out of gratitude for His remembrance, by His permission. This is an allusion to the fact that the student needs the permission and certification of the shaykhs (masha'ikh), and that the greatest of ailments is that a person limits himself to what he has and does not seek more of the best provision (khayr al-zad) from what he does not have. Then the Exalted said: ﴿So remind﴾, that is, with this wise reminder. He expressed it with the particle of doubt to convey universal generality, so He said: ﴿if the reminder benefits﴾, that is, if you deem its benefit possible and hope for it, even if it is in a weak manner, as indicated by the feminine form of the verb after the particle of doubt has conveyed (that meaning). Undoubtedly, a person, because he does not know the unseen, does not definitively rule out the benefit of anyone; rather he remains in hope of it, even if he considers it unlikely. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) would never cease calling to Allah, the Exalted, however severe the matter became, and he would not belittle anyone whom he invited, nor despair of anyone, however harsh he was towards him. As for the command to turn away from those who turn away and the like, it refers only to turning away from grieving over them and from wearing oneself out in sorrow over them and the like.

When He commanded him to remind everyone, He divided people with respect to it into two categories: one category accepts the reminder, and the other does not accept it, to make known that He, glory be to Him and exalted, knows each of the two categories, as a whole and individually, specifically. He has always been knowing of that, but He did not specify it as a trial from Him for His servants, so that the proof would be established against them by what they recognize among themselves, and His is the conclusive proof. So He said, urging the thanks for the calamities [of - ] the intellect and the like, and of the limbs, from the heart and the tongue and other than these: ﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits﴾, meaning, with a promise that does not fail, even if in the most hidden of the ways of reminding, which the idgham (assimilation) indicates. ﴿Whoever fears﴾, meaning: there is in his natural disposition some kind of fear, and he is the one who is fortunate, because of the great happiness that has been decreed for him in himself, to accept the upright, easy religion. So he recalls what he knows of it in himself and takes admonition, for fear leads to every good. Thus he enjoys, with his heart and body, in the highest Garden, and he lives in it a good life, without sickness or affliction, forever, without end or termination.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 87, verse 11:

When he had mentioned those who love for the sake of God (fi Allah) their love, he mentioned those who hate for the sake of God. The sign of love is following (iqtida'), and the sign of hatred is avoidance (tajannub), refusal (intiha'), innovation (ibtida') and refusal to submit (aba'). So He said: ﴿And he shall avoid it﴾, meaning he compels his soul and his original, upright disposition (fitrah) to avoid the reminder (dhikra) by which We intend to admonish him, [a reminder brought] from the most noble of creation and the greatest of them in connection with the Creator. And since this one who works on straightening his soul by force is extremely obstinate (shadid al-utuww), He said: ﴿the most wretched﴾, meaning the one who bears this description absolutely, because he opposed the most noble of the messengers. He does not fear, so he is the most wretched of people, just as whoever believed in him (p-400) is more excellent than those who believed in the messengers before him, upon them be prayers and peace.

When He mentioned his attribute that required him to do evil deeds, He mentioned his recompense, saying: ﴿Who will burn in﴾, that is, he will directly undergo the burning [with his heart -] and with his body, enduring ﴿the greatest Fire﴾ [that is -] which is the greatest of the levels and is the lowest, because it is not in his nature to fear, but he is like the hardest stone, because he is ignorant and blindly imitative, or arrogant and obstinate. Or the intended meaning is the Fire of the Hereafter, for it is greater than the Fire of the barzakh (the intermediate realm between death and resurrection) and greater than the Fire of this world by seventy parts. Therefore it deserves to be described by the elative form (af'al al-tafdil) without restriction. This verse is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which one element is mentioned and its opposite is omitted, and vice versa): in the first part He mentioned the fruit, which is fear (khashyah), as evidence for the omission of its opposite in the second part, which is hardness (qaswah) arising from the judgment of wretchedness. In the second part He mentioned the root and cause, which is wretchedness, as evidence for the omission of its opposite in the first part, which is happiness (sa'adah). So bringing about happiness is a cause and fear is a fruit, and bringing about wretchedness is a cause and hardness is a fruit and effect. Likewise is what springs from the Fire and what arises from it. The secret of this is that [He -] mentioned the origin of happiness first, to urge toward it, and the outcome of wretchedness second, to warn against it. Al-Malawi said: There is no doubt that the Mighty Qur'an is at the highest level of eloquence in composition and wondrous arrangement (p-401), and abundance of meanings together with brevity and absence of repetition. So in one place it suffices with the fruit without the cause, and in another with the cause without the fruit, because the first indicates the second and the second indicates the first. Thus it joins the cause to the fruit and the fruit to the cause, just as qada' (divine decree) is mentioned and used in place of qadar (divine measure), and qadar is mentioned and used in place of qada'. Similarly, the judgment (hukm) is mentioned while the other two are left out, and it points to them. Thus all three are mentioned. This becomes clear through an example: whoever wants to set up a waterwheel first plans the location of the well with its pivot, its gear, its axle, and its basin into which the passer-by pours, and its channels from which the water flows. This planning is design, arrangement, judgment, and will. When he has done that and completed it, it is called decree (qada'), creation, and effect. When he installs on the mountains buckets that carry a measured amount of water, which, when they descend into the water, take it up, and when they rise and reach the top and wish to descend, they empty it, thus directing the water from its channels to what it was made for, that is the measure (qadar), and it is the end. So whenever one of the three is mentioned, namely the judgment, the decree, and the measure, it indicates the others.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 87, verse 13:

Since one whose condition is such as this would perish, according to what is customary, in the quickest time, then if it is among his condition, together with this immensity, that he does not perish, that would be clear evidence that no one knows the true extent of the greatness of the One who decrees it except Him, glorified and exalted be He. So He pointed to this by using the particle of delay (thumma), to inform that the degrees of this severity in oscillating (p-402) between death and life, the height of which because of the intensity of the burning, none knows except Allah, the Exalted. So He said: ﴿Then he will neither die therein﴾, meaning, no death will be renewed for him in this fire, however long the span.

And since one who enters the Fire, whom its burning does not affect in terms of death, might be honored by that as a breach of customary norms, He guarded against this by His saying: ﴿nor will he live﴾, meaning, a life that benefits him, because he did not purify himself, so he neither affirmed the truth nor prayed.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 87, verse 14:

When this was established, that for this [state] there is this greatest wretchedness, the implied sense was: because he did not purify himself, since he was [naturally] imprinted with fear [of God], there necessarily produces His saying, exalted is He, indicating the obligatory religion, which is abstention (ijtinab) and acquisition (ijtilab). He combined abstention and acquisition through purification, through devotion to the Gates and constant attendance at the Thresholds, through carrying out the command and avoiding the prohibition, through the striving (mujahadat) that bring one near to Him, glorified and exalted is He, the things that save after what He warned against of the things that destroy, for hastening toward His loves and His pleasures, in unity upon worship that connects to the Creator, after the attainment of perfection and completion. For there is necessarily, in the good life, after attachment to the One of the vast dignity and emulation of the one who does not swerve, a bond by a most excellent way through which one obtains felicity, so that one reaches the intended goal, fills his times with their duties, lest any deficiency or waste of precious times occur to him, or any heedlessness (p-403) by which the highway robbers seize him. ﴿He has certainly succeeded﴾, meaning he has attained every aim, ﴿who purifies himself﴾, meaning he works at purifying himself from corrupt beliefs, morals, sayings, deeds and wealth, and at developing his inward and outward works, and giving charity from his wealth. That is the glorification (tasbih) which was commanded at the beginning of the surah and what was transmitted from it. Whoever acts upon this, then he is the most fortunate.

When the greatest of the deeds that purify are remembrance and prayer, God Most High said: ﴿And remembers﴾, i.e., with the heart and the tongue, dhikr and dhukr (both with a kasra and a damma) ﴿the name of his Lord﴾, i.e., the attributes of the One who has been good to him. For when he remembers the attribute, he is gladdened by it, so his inner self overflows onto his outer self with the mention of the word that indicates it. And when he mentions the word, which is the name that indicates it, the remembrance of the named is impressed upon his heart. ﴿And prays﴾, i.e., the legally prescribed prayer (ṣalāh), because it is the greatest remembrance. So it is the greatest of the bodily acts of worship, just as zakat is the greatest of the acts of worship concerning wealth. Whoever does this is relieved of the disease of self-admiration (i'jāb) and of what follows it of deficiencies that bring about a bad reversal. He is characterized by the moral qualities of God mentioned at the beginning of the surah: emptying himself of deficiencies through purification (tazkiyah), and adorning himself with perfections through remembrance and prayer. For, because of His greatness, none is qualified to remember Him except one who persists in [remembering] His name, so he does not wretch, and does not burn in the Greatest Fire, by a promise that admits no breach. The verse is an instance of ihtibāk (a rhetorical device in which one element is omitted and its counterpart is left to be understood): it mentioned first the burning as evidence for omitting its opposite in the second part, and second the purification as evidence for omitting its opposite in the first part. The mention of purification and remembrance has covered this, and prayer is among the means of treatment by ripening, then by drinks, then by foods. The verse is suitable to be taken as referring to zakat al-fiṭr and to the takbīrs of the Eid and its prayer, even though the surah is Meccan and fasting was prescribed in Medina, because what matters is the generality of the wording, given God's comprehensive knowledge, glory be to Him, of the past, the present and the future alike. Al-Rāzī said in al-Lawāmi': Zakat al-fiṭr is given before the Eid prayer. Ibn Mas'ūd (may God be pleased with him) used to say: "May God have mercy on a person who gives charity and then prays," and then he would recite this verse. And even though the surah is Meccan, it is possible that the revelation preceded the ruling, as God said: ﴿And you are a lawful [dweller] in this city﴾ [al-Balad: 2], and the surah is Meccan, and the effect of this lawfulness appeared on the Day of the Conquest. End of quotation, and he took it from al-Baghawī. Al-Baghawī added that Ibn 'Umar (may God be pleased with him and his father) used to instruct Nāfi' (may God be pleased with him) to do something similar to what Ibn Mas'ūd said, and he would say: "This verse was only revealed concerning this." Al-Bazzār narrated: "From 'Awf ibn Mālik al-Ashja'ī (may God be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he used to order zakat al-fiṭr to be given before praying the Eid prayer, and would recite this verse." In its chain is Kuthayyir ibn 'Abd Allāh (p-405). al-Tirmidhī graded him ḥasan, while others weakened him. And God knows best.

Since the sense is "And you do not do that," or "they do not do it," according to both readings, He connected to it His words, in the majority reading, in the address form, by way of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person), which indicates the extremity of [the anger -]. This alerts to the treatments through the cause of the fourth remedy, which is *istifragh* (purgation), by negating the vices and corruptions, by censuring what one should be free of, and by urging what must be attained, so as to attain good care: ﴿Rather, you prefer﴾, that is, you choose and single out for yourselves exclusively, O wretched ones. And "the unseen" [is read] as in the original form according to Abu 'Amr: ﴿the life of this world﴾, that is, the base one, passing away, the one present, while it is [evil and -] transient, occupying yourselves with it because of its presence, like the animals that are bound to the sensible things. So your preoccupation with it has consumed your times and prevented you from the remembrance of the name of God, which is prohibited, and from the remembrance of God that prepares for it, and from purifying your souls. Thus that has brought upon you the disease of *al-qubqub* (the belly) and *al-dubdub* (the private part), and the love of wealth, which leads to the worst of deeds, ﴿and you neglect the Hereafter﴾.

﴿And the Hereafter﴾ [i.e. -] while the abode that is the ultimate goal of creation and the aim of the command, the exalted (p-406), free from frivolity, exempt from departing from wisdom, is ﴿better﴾ i.e. [than -] this world, on the assumption of granting it, because in it there is good, since its bliss is pure, with no turbidity in it in any respect, ﴿and more enduring﴾ i.e. than it, on the assumption of the impossible, in this world, in that its prolongation until the time of its cessation is called permanence. The bliss of the Hereafter is lasting, with no cessation at all, and what is lasting is not equated with what passes away in any respect. Whoever knows this, and it is a matter that is not unknown, occupies himself with what attains the Hereafter and negates this world in its two divisions: the sensible objects and the immaterial desires, the psychological vanities and the imagined pleasures. The verse contains ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which one element is mentioned and its counterpart is left implied, and vice versa): mentioning preference and the lowly first indicates abandonment and the exalted second, and mentioning good and permanence second indicates their opposites first. The secret of this is that none prefers the base except a base person, so He mentioned it first because it is more effective in producing aversion, and He mentioned good and permanence second because it is more effective in producing desire.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 87, verse 18:

Since this outcome, which is success (al-falah) through purification (tazkiyah, the cleansing of the soul) and what follows from it, is the essence of the revealed Books, through which the first existence is organized, he described it, to encourage attention to it, with the attribute of the collection of antiquity (jam' al-qidam), which entails soundness through the succession of thoughts across the passage of ages. The reason is that what the years have passed over, and what the eras have endured in being accepted, is more readily accepted by the soul (al-nafs aqbal li-l-idh'an [lahu -]) and more apt to bind it. Along with antiquity, he also indicated that the one to whom it was revealed, (ﷺ), is not an innovation among the Messengers, peace be upon them, but is upon their path. Therefore, rejecting his message among theirs is not said by any fair-minded person, especially since he has surpassed them in miracles and [all -] marvels. He emphasized, for the sake of the one who denies, saying: ﴿Indeed, this﴾, that is, this great admonition in the glorification that was mentioned in these surahs, and what results from it of purification through remembrance, which necessitates prayer, turning away from the world, and turning toward the Hereafter, because it comprises every good. It is established in every law, because it is the aim of the ruling, so it does not accept abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one). ﴿Is in the former scrolls﴾. So whoever follows this Qur'an, which is in these divine scrolls, has adorned himself with the ornament of speech through the eloquence it conveys, which is in utmost precision and great significance, and through what it knows of the unseen, whether it is occurring or has occurred, which the people of these times have forgotten. Thus he is spared the misguidance of poets and soothsayers, who fall into sin and transgression. The Qur'an combines superlative praise, delicate amatory prelude (nasib) in describing the dark-eyed maidens and the wine, passionate boasting, eloquent satire (hija') against the enemies of God, attractive encouragement that draws hearts, and warning, along with the informative sayings, the legal prescribed punishments (hudud), and other matters that poets cannot reach, and to whose lowest reaches the eloquence of the eloquent does not attain.

(p-408) When that was the case, he was singled out from among them to magnify the rank of this admonition, the greatest of the earlier prophets. He said, substituting [a word] and pointing to inference by experience: ﴿the scrolls of Ibrahim﴾, his name coming first, because his scrolls are closer to admonition, as the hadith of Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, states. ﴿And Musa﴾ is mentioned last, because the predominant character of his book is legal rulings, and admonitions in it are few. Among them are the forceful warnings, such as the curse upon whoever opposes the commands of the Torah (al-Tawrat), the greatest of which is the glad tidings of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the report that they would oppose it, as [it is -] mentioned at its end. Yet the mention of the two Prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, follows the原 order of existence and excellence. The last of them urged tazkiyah (purification), which is cleansing oneself from impurities, the meaning of tanzih (declaring Allah free of imperfection) and taking on the character traits of Allah to the extent of one's capacity. In his coming and in the reminder of it there is an announcement that Allah, exalted is He, did not leave creation without clarification [after He created them], because He did not create them aimlessly, since that would be futility (ʿabath), which is among the greatest deficiencies [and He, glorified is He, is exempt from all traces of deficiency]. Thus the last of it returns to the first of it. The declaration of the Lord's transcendence, glorified and exalted is He, and the purification of the self are both the ultimate aim of its bearing. And Allah is the Granter of success to what is right, and to Him is the return and the final resort.
